name: Changsha Mahjong
description: Changsha Mahjong is a Chinese regional Mahjong variant associated with Changsha and surrounding Hunan play communities. It preserves classic draw-discard meld structure while following local rule profiles and scoring expectations.

overview.description: Changsha Mahjong is a Chinese regional Mahjong variant associated with Changsha and surrounding Hunan play communities. It preserves classic draw-discard meld structure while following local rule profiles and scoring expectations.

history.origins: Changsha Mahjong developed as a regional expression of Chinese Mahjong play with local table preferences for pacing and hand valuation.
timeline: 20th century: regional table rules spread through local social play.
Modern era: regional profiles documented and implemented online with stable conventions.
history.cultural: It is played as a social table game in Changsha and wider Hunan communities.
history.evolution: Local rule profiles vary by table, but the draw-discard core remains consistent with broader Mahjong traditions.

setup.deck: Standard Mahjong set with suited tiles, honor tiles, and bonus tiles according to table profile.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 13 tiles; dealer receives 14 and discards first.

rules.objective: Complete a legal winning hand and satisfy the active Changsha scoring profile.
rules.gameplay: Players draw one tile and discard one tile in turn. Discards may be claimed for legal melds under claim priority rules. A hand wins on self-draw or discard claim when the hand structure and the profile's scoring validity are satisfied.
keyRules: Normal turn rhythm is draw then discard.
Claim legality and priority govern Chow, Pung, and Kong interruptions.
Winning requires valid hand structure and accepted profile scoring.

strategy.basic: Keep efficient waits and avoid committing to narrow shapes too early.
strategy.intermediate: Track visible tiles and opponent tempo to decide when to push or defend.
strategy.advanced: Pivot between speed and value routes based on tile flow and opponent threat signals.
tips: Prefer two-sided waits when completion speed is critical.
Switch to defensive discards when an opponent accelerates through visible commitments.
